Deuteronomy 4: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, looking back to Horeb (Sinai), where the covenant was made with the previous generation. The Baal-peor episode (4:3) occurred shortly before, in Numbers 25.
Deuteronomy 5: Moses addresses the new generation on the plains of Moab, recalling the giving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb (Exodus 20 gives the earlier account).
Deuteronomy 12: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. This chapter begins the 'statutes and rules' section (chapters 12-26), which applies the covenant to life in the land.
Joshua 5: Israel is camped at Gilgal near Jericho. The wilderness generation had died, and the new generation had not undergone the covenant sign of circumcision according to the text (5:5).
Joshua 7: The story takes place near Jericho and the hill country to the west. Ai (meaning 'the ruin') is located near Bethel (7:2). Its exact location is debated; candidates include et-Tell, Khirbet el-Maqatir, and others. The Valley of Achor lies near Jericho.
Joshua 8: Ai lies in the central hill country near Bethel. Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim overlook Shechem, about 20 miles (30 km) north of Ai, where Moses had commanded a ceremony (Deuteronomy 11:29–30; 27:1–8).
Joshua 9: Gibeon is about 6 miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem, generally identified with el-Jib. Excavations there uncovered a large water system and wine-making installations, along with jar handles inscribed with 'Gibeon' (gb'n) from the Iron Age. These discoveries support the location but do not date or confirm the treaty itself.
Joshua 10: The battle begins at Gibeon and moves west and south through the Valley of Aijalon, Beth-horon, Azekah, and Makkedah, then to Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. These are in the hill country and Shephelah of what became Judah. The Amarna letters (14th century BC) show Jerusalem ruled by a local king, Abdi-Heba, who was a vassal of Egypt, illustrating that city-state kings existed in this area, though they do not refer to Joshua.
Joshua 12: The list covers the Transjordan, the Jordan Valley, the hill country, the Shephelah, and the coast and plains in the north. Canaan was divided among many small city-states, a pattern known from the Amarna letters (14th century BC).
Joshua 24: Shechem lies in the hill country of Ephraim between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and is identified with Tell Balata. It had earlier links to Abraham (Genesis 12:6–7) and Jacob (Genesis 33:18–20). The Hebrew text says the people assembled at Shechem, while some Greek manuscripts read Shiloh. The speech follows the form of ancient treaties, beginning with a historical review.
Joshua 2: Shittim (also called Abel-shittim) lies on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan; Jericho is a walled city just west of the river, in the Jordan Valley. The site is commonly identified with Tell es-Sultan. Canaan in the Late Bronze Age was a collection of city-states, as reflected in the Amarna letters from Egypt (14th century BC).
Judges 1: After Joshua's death, the tribes fight separately for their territories, and many Canaanite towns remain (Judges 1:27–33). Judges covers the time before Israel had a king, usually placed in the early Iron Age, about 1200–1050 BC.
Judges 2: A new generation grows up "which knew not the LORD" (Judges 2:10). The chapter sets out the cycle that repeats through the book: idolatry, oppression, crying out, and a deliverer.
Judges 3: Othniel defeats Chushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia; Ehud kills Eglon king of Moab at Jericho, "the city of palm trees" (Judges 3:13); Shamgar fights the Philistines.
Judges 4: Jabin king of Canaan rules from Hazor, with Sisera commanding nine hundred iron chariots (Judges 4:3). Deborah judges under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel.
Judges 5: Deborah and Barak's song celebrates the victory by the river Kishon. It is often considered among the oldest poetry in the Bible.
Judges 6: Midianites and Amalekites raid Israel at harvest for seven years, camels and all (Judges 6:3–5). Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress at Ophrah to hide it.
Judges 7: Gideon camps by the well of Harod with three hundred men; the Midianites lie in the valley below the hill of Moreh, in the Jezreel valley.
Judges 8: Gideon pursues the Midianite kings east across the Jordan to Succoth and Penuel, then returns to Ophrah. The land has rest forty years (Judges 8:28).
Judges 9: Gideon's son Abimelech makes himself king at Shechem for three years and dies attacking the tower of Thebez.
Judges 10: Tola and Jair judge Israel. The Ammonites oppress Gilead, east of the Jordan, for eighteen years (Judges 10:8).
Judges 11: Jephthah of Gilead fights Ammon. He says Israel has held the land for three hundred years (Judges 11:26).
Judges 12: Ephraim fights Jephthah's Gileadites at the Jordan fords, where the password "Shibboleth" exposes the Ephraimites (Judges 12:6).
Judges 13: The Philistines rule Israel for forty years (Judges 13:1). Samson is born to Manoah of Zorah, a Danite town in the foothills bordering Philistine land.
Judges 14: Samson goes down to Timnath to marry a Philistine woman. Timnah has been identified with Tel Batash in the Sorek valley.
Judges 15: Samson burns Philistine grain at harvest and kills a thousand men at Ramathlehi in Judah.
Judges 16: Samson visits Gaza, falls to Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and dies in the temple of Dagon at Gaza. He judged Israel twenty years (Judges 16:31).
Judges 17: "In those days there was no king in Israel" (Judges 17:6). Micah of mount Ephraim sets up a shrine and hires a Levite from Bethlehem.
Judges 18: The Danites, still without land, move north and take Laish, renaming it Dan. Tel Dan, near the sources of the Jordan, has been excavated.
Judges 19: A Levite travels from Bethlehem with his concubine and stays at Gibeah in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem, which was then "Jebus" (Judges 19:10).
Judges 20: The tribes gather at Mizpeh and fight Benjamin at Gibeah. The ark of the covenant is at Bethel "in those days" (Judges 20:27), with Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, as priest.
Judges 21: The tribes find wives for Benjamin's survivors from Jabeshgilead and from the yearly feast at Shiloh.
Ruth 1: The story is set "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). Elimelech's family moves from Bethlehem in Judah to Moab, east of the Dead Sea, during a famine.
Ruth 2: Ruth gleans in Boaz's field near Bethlehem from the barley harvest through the wheat harvest (Ruth 2:23), roughly April to June.
Ruth 3: Boaz winnows barley at night on the threshing floor at Bethlehem (Ruth 3:2).
Ruth 4: Boaz settles the matter before ten elders at Bethlehem's gate. The book ends with a genealogy from Pharez to David (Ruth 4:18–22).
